title: "Getting started"
description: "Install sportsdataverse and pull your first tidy DataFrame of real ESPN data."
jupyter: python3
---

`sportsdataverse` is the Python sister to the SportsDataverse R packages
(`hoopR`, `wehoop`, `cfbfastR`, `fastRhockey`, `baseballr`). It provides tidy
access to play-by-play, box score, schedule, roster, and odds data across the
NBA, WNBA, NFL, College Football, Men's and Women's College Basketball, MLB,
and NHL.

## Install

::: {.panel-tabset}

### pip

```bash
pip install sportsdataverse
```

### uv

```bash
uv add sportsdataverse
```

### conda

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge sportsdataverse
```

:::

Every `espn_<sport>_*` function returns a [polars](https://pola.rs) `DataFrame`
by default. Pass `return_as_pandas=True` for a pandas frame instead.

## Your first call

The cell below runs **at documentation build time** against the live ESPN API,
so the table you see is the genuine output of the function — not a
hand-maintained snapshot that can silently drift out of date.

```{python}
import polars as pl
pl.Config.set_tbl_rows(6)
pl.Config.set_tbl_cols(6)

from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_teams

teams = espn_nba_teams()
teams.select(
    ["team_id", "team_location", "team_name", "team_display_name", "team_abbreviation"]
).head(6)
```

That is all 30 NBA franchises with their ESPN ids — the `team_id` column is the
key you pass to roster and schedule calls.

```{python}
print(f"espn_nba_teams() returned {teams.shape[0]} rows x {teams.shape[1]} columns")
```

## The same shape across every sport

The cross-league surface is uniform: swap the sport slug and the call works the
same way. Here is the women's college basketball team list, again executed
live:

```{python}
from sportsdataverse.wbb import espn_wbb_teams

wbb = espn_wbb_teams()
print(f"espn_wbb_teams() -> {wbb.shape[0]} teams")
wbb.select(["team_id", "team_display_name", "team_abbreviation"]).head(5)
```
